title: A yeast bud arises where surface tension locally and suddenly diminishes

fields.label: Label
fields.value: A yeast bud arises where surface tension locally and suddenly diminishes

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: A bud appears on a yeast cell because the surface tension diminishes at one part of the cell surface, so that this area expands, after which the bud's own surface tension rounds it into a roughly spherical form.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: When a “bud” appears, whether with or without actual growth by osmosis or otherwise of the mass, it does so because at a certain part of the cell-surface the surface tension has more or less suddenly diminished, and the area of that portion expands accordingly

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter V, “The Forms of Cells”; topic “Budding yeast and localised tension changes”. Scope: budding yeast cells

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch05-07: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.69

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The proposed temporal sequence and localized mechanical cause are experimentally discriminating. Existing imaging can test morphology and molecular order, but direct tension measurements needed for confirmation are limited.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure local membrane or wall tension before and during yeast bud emergence and perturb tension locally while imaging polarity markers. Support requires a local tension drop preceding and inducing expansion, followed by tension-dependent rounding; polarity-driven growth without the predicted drop refutes it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Direct local tension reporters are uncommon in archived yeast data.

Cell-wall remodeling and polarized actin are strong alternative mechanisms.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.7
operationalizability: 0.8
analysis feasibility: 0.65
discriminating power: 0.75
data adequacy: 0.55

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Yeast budding is heavily imaged and genetically annotated, so the geometric sequence, local expansion then rounding, is testable now. The causal claim is a sudden local fall in surface tension, and the archived variables are genes and shapes rather than tension. Landmark mutants provide a serious rival, which makes the available test informative but one step removed from the force Thompson names.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: At the future bud site on a yeast cell, measure local surface tension through bud emergence and test whether a local drop precedes expansion, as against a polarity landmark that directs growth at constant tension. A tension drop that is necessary and sufficient for the bud would support the claim; budding at a marked site with no tension drop, or failure of budding when tension is locally reduced away from the landmark, would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Phenotype databases record shape and gene, not local tension.

Coverage is excellent for Saccharomyces and thin for other budding yeasts.

Turgor-driven expansion and a tension drop make similar early bulges.
